title: Former Notre Dame, current Commanders QB Sam Hartman to star in new season of 'The Bachelor' - CBS Sports
description: Hartman is currently on Washington's practice squad
body:
Hartman is currently on Washington's practice squad
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 13, 2026
                            
                    at
    9:57 am ET
                        
                •
            
            1 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Sam Hartman is swapping his helmet for a suit, and instead of footballs, the Commanders quarterback will soon be passing out roses. The 27-year-old has been named as the next star of "The Bachelor," as the ABC series kicks off its 30th season in March 2027. Following Washington's Week 10 victory over the New York Giants on Thursday night, Hartman was on "Good Morning America" on Friday morning for the official announcement.  "I'm excited but also very nervous," Hartman said, via ABC News. He added: "I have a tough time holding conversation with one girl — 30 is going to be pretty tough."
As noted by NFL Network, the show is slated to shoot early in 2027 over the course of the offseason, so Hartman's day job doesn't appear to be impacted by him starring in the show. Hartman, who is currently on the Commanders practice squad, has been with Washington ever since he signed with the franchise as an undrafted free agent out of Notre Dame in 2024. Over the course of his tenure with the organization, he's volleyed between the active roster and the practice squad. Hartman has yet to make an appearance in an NFL regular season game. At the collegiate level, Hartman started his career at Wake Forest before transferring to Notre Dame for his final season in 2023 before opting for the pros. At Wake Forest, he was All-ACC second team in 2021 and All-ACC third team in 2022. During the 2022 season, Hartman was awarded the Brian Piccolo Award for the "most courageous" player in the ACC following a diagnosis of Paget-Schroetter syndrome, a condition that causes blood clots in a vein near the collarbone. That required Hartman to undergo surgery, but the quarterback missed only one game. 
Hartman played 48 games at Wake Forest and is the program's all-time leading passer with 12,967 yards. Over his lone season at Notre Dame in 2023, he led the Fighting Irish to a 9-3 record while completing 63.5% of his throws for 2,689 yards, 24 touchdowns, and just eight interceptions.

title: Can Mauricio Pochettino replicate hallmark intensity he brought to USMNT with Manchester United? - CBS Sports
description: The Red Devils are the Premier League's least athletic team by some measures, posing a massive tactical roadblock
body:
The Red Devils are the Premier League's least athletic team by some measures, posing a massive tactical roadblock for a manager built on relentless pressing
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 13, 2026
                            
                    at
    7:43 am ET
                        
                •
            
            5 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        From the jump, we should say, physical metrics are not going to tell you the whole story about any player, team or tactical system. Indeed, there is such potential for misdiagnosis when assessing running statistics that senior figures at more than one of the best recruiting clubs in England consider their worth to be, at best, dubious.Too often, sprints are used as a proxy for effort when anyone who has even passing familiarity with the sport of soccer knows better. You know who didn't have to peg it all that often? Sergio Busquets, perhaps the best defensive midfielder of his generation, plying his trade for the majority of his career at Barcelona. Keep the ball, read the game, control the territory and you will very quickly find the other team covering plenty more kilometers than you.Manchester United didn't slide into the bottom three because they were eating up less ground per game, 112.5 kilometers to be precise, than 18 of the other 19 teams in the Premier League this season. If there were any correlation between distance covered and results, then the relegation race would be even more exciting than it is shaping up to be, given that Liverpool sit below United on that measure and Manchester City above them. It is quite hard to believe that United are winning fewer games compared to last year (when they had nearly 10% less possession it should be noted) because each player is covering about 45 meters fewer per game.  Physical data might not be linked to team quality, then, but it might tell us something relevant if, for instance, United were to hire a coach who prizes dynamic players and demands an intense press at the very top of the pitch. A Mauricio Pochettino type, if you will. The soon-to-be former United States men's national team head coach, handed the task of extricating Manchester United from the relegation zone before molding a contender, is defined by the aggression and energy of his charges. It is why he was the perfect match for a young Tottenham side with a point to prove. It is why Paris Saint-Germain and the Neymar-Kylian Mbappe axis was such an obviously awkward fit from the off.
        
            
                USMNT coaching candidates: Could Pep Guardiola potentially replace Mauricio Pochettino?
                
                    Chuck Booth                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
It is also a template that has worked even when there was cause for skepticism. You couldn't have players sprinting their way across SoFi after the rigors of a club season, said those who doubted the USMNT. He didn't ask much of his team, just "to use your brain while physically, you were killing yourself," as Tim Ream, then 38, said in the summer.
Tell you what, though, it worked. The United States' World Cup campaign might have ended at about the time and in the fashion that most expected, but at their best, they were pressing dynamos. Their 10.16 passes allowed per defensive action (PPDA) -- a measure of press intensity -- placed them sixth among the 48 teams at the World Cup, rubbing shoulders with the likes of Germany, Spain and Uruguay, coached by Pochettino's mentor and high priest of the high press Marcelo Bielsa. No team that reached the knockouts forced their opponents to misplace a higher proportion of their passes than the U.S., 22.8%.Pochettino might have framed much of his work around changing the culture of the USMNT, but that was a job that was easier to do with a player pool that suited his needs. His squad was strong, organized and, most importantly of all, athletic.That is not a term that is particularly associated with Manchester United. Indeed, according to Gradient Sports, one of the leading external providers of physical data in football, Pochettino's new team is the least athletic in the Premier League. Based on Gradient's athleticism score -- which combines a host of physical data points including accelerations and decelerations, sprint distance and max speed -- United and Nottingham Forest are cut adrift from the rest of the league. In average max speed of outfield players, United also rank 19th out of 20, 5% slower than the fleet-footed Bournemouth and Liverpool. 

                                                                    Gradient Sports
                                                            The months to come may prove that United look unathletic because that's how Michael Carrick wanted them to play, controlling possession and building more steadily than the sides who rushed headfirst into any counter that came their way. Instinctively, though, that does not feel like the United of Harry Maguire, Youri Tielemans and Kobbie Mainoo, does it?The three center backs who have started the bulk of United's Premier League games this season -- Maguire, Lisandro Martinez and Ayden Heaven -- all rank around the bottom third or lower of players in their position in terms of top speed, accelerations and decelerations and percentage of runs at high speeds (20-25 km/h), according to Gradient data. It is a similar story for the midfielders, particularly Andrey Santos, Mainoo and Tielemans. The one central midfield option with an impressive athletic profile, Carlos Baleba, is out injured. It seemed bitterly ironic that Baleba's hamstring went after a driving run through midfield. The sheer act of high-intensity running does sometimes look like it puts an unbearable strain on United legs.That might be why they do it so little. Opta judges that Santos applies pressure to 56.2% of his opponents' touches, Tielemans 56.8%, Bruno Fernandes 57% and Mainoo 57.3%. All of them sit in the bottom 12 in the league among midfielders with 300 or more minutes. Marcus Rashford, Bryan Mbeumo, Matheus Cunha and Amad Diallo occupy spots one, three, five and six in terms of the top flight's least pressing-y forwards.
Now, of course, Pochettino can adapt. After all, he has just implemented a surprisingly effective high press in a side captained by Ream (sorry, Tim!). A lot of the Chelsea squad he took over in 2023-24 did not look to be at ease hunting the ball, but he still had them above league average in PPDA, opponent pass completion, ball recoveries and in particular duel success in the final third. A bit more oomph is not beyond these United players, as they showed last season.However, it is particularly curious to finally alight on Pochettino, whom they could have hired at least half a dozen times in the past, when the squad seems so ill-suited to his principles. We might not be able to tell from physical data whether this team was giving its all for Carrick -- and, by extension, whether there is another gear for the new manager to drive them to -- but what we can see is certainly enough to raise the question of why the powers that be at United think that this is a squad ready to play Pochettino-style.

title: UFC 334: How Kayla Harrison overcame neck injury for dream fight with Amanda Nunes - CBS Sports
description: NEW YORK -- As Kayla Harrison closes in on the biggest fight of her career on Saturday in arguably the most prestigious women's matchup
body:
NEW YORK -- As Kayla Harrison closes in on the biggest fight of her career on Saturday in arguably the most prestigious women's matchup in the sport's history, it's difficult for her not to reflect back upon the battle that led up to it. Harrison (19-1), the 36-year-old UFC bantamweight champion, will take on former champion and teammate Amanda Nunes (23-5), the greatest female fighter of all time, in the co-main event of UFC 334 inside Madison Square Garden. The fight was originally scheduled for January at UFC 324 until Harrison withdrew just 11 days before. After years of competing through herniated discs in her neck dating back to her days as a two-time U.S. Olympic gold medalist in judo, Harrison suffered an injury in training so severe that it required immediate surgery. And her road to rehabilitation was so daunting and painful that she battled with the possibility that a full recovery might not be in the cards. "It was a wrench that I was not expecting in the plans, but God is good," Harrison told CBS Sports on Tuesday. "The recovery was a lot harder than I anticipated, so I'm very grateful to be here this week. I have been humbled and I'm hungry. I'm hungrier than I think I have been in a long time. I have no doubt that it all happened for a reason. Who I am as a result of that hurdle and obstacle in my life has propelled me to even greater heights as a person, as a mother and as a fighter. I'm excited to showcase it."
As Harrison put it, the physical trials she endured throughout her recovery left her in a position to really question how badly she wanted to come back for what might prove to be the final bout of her eight-year pro MMA career. Harrison hasn't yet ruled either way, but has maintained that the end is near, and that a retirement after Saturday for her, win or lose, remains a possibility.For as much as Nunes, the only female two-division champion in UFC history who went on to defend both titles simultaneously, will need to shake off three years of cage rust following her 2023 retirement due to physical burnout, Harrison will be returning to the Octagon for the first time in 17 months since submitting Julianna Pena in June 2025 at UFC 316 to win the 135-pound title. 
A native of Middletown, Ohio, who now lives and trains in South Florida, Harrison said that the prospect of finally facing off against Nunes is the only reason she endured the recovery from neck surgery to put on the gloves one more time. Had her injury postponed an upcoming fight against anyone else, she would've walked away for good. The reason is simple. From the first time she set foot inside an MMA gym in late 2016, Harrison maintained she was only entering the sport to become the best to ever do it. By the time she made her pro debut in 2018 as a teammate of Nunes at American Top Team in Coconut Creek, Florida, "The Lioness" was months away from knocking out Cris Cyborg in the biggest fight in women's MMA history and cementing her status as the GOAT.So, should Harrison defeat Nunes, the GOAT, on Saturday in a long-awaited matchup that has been talked about for so many years (and led to Nunes leaving ATT in early 2022), a victory would make Harrison what? 
"The GOAT," Harrison said. "I mean, I think so."
Not every historian will completely agree. For as unique as her career has been, whether it was winning a pair of 155-pound tournaments (and $1 million prizes) with the PFL or the three wins she has recorded as a bantamweight since making her UFC debut in 2024, Harrison doesn't have anywhere near the number of legendary names on her resume akin to Nunes.What Harrison has been, however, is completely dominant, winning 19 of her 20 pro fights, with the only defeat – a five-round unanimous decision to Larissa Pacheco in the finals of the 2022 PFL lightweight tournament – coming on an off night to an opponent she had soundly defeated twice in the previous three years. "I have come to peace with my career," Harrison said. "It's something that I really had to wrestle with when I was recovering from the injury, not knowing if this fight was ever going to happen. I'm at peace with my career and happy with everything. Six-year-old me could never have dreamed of this life that I live. I am eternally grateful and this is the fight that I have wanted since I started MMA.
"A lot of things had to go right in order for this to happen, and some things did go wrong and it's still happening. I'm grateful to Amanda and I just feel really blessed. When you look at my life, sometimes I can't believe it. I really can't. It has been full of a lot of lows but so many more highs. And to be the GOAT, that was the goal from Day 1."Harrison's personal story has long been one about perseverance. Abused by her judo coach as a youth, she went on to raise awareness as an advocate for child sexual abuse. She also became a single mother after adopting her niece and nephew and serves as their homeschool teacher. Harrison's life of sacrifice extends to her unique fighting legacy when you factor in the seemingly insurmountable weight cut she was forced to make to realize her UFC dreams. 
After competing in judo on the Olympic level at 172 pounds, Harrison initially cut down to 155 pounds to compete as a lightweight with PFL. But the UFC folded its 145-pound featherweight division following Nunes' retirement, which meant Harrison needed to cut an additional 20 pounds to make the bantamweight. The fact that Harrison successfully did so even once shows how badly becoming a UFC champion has been part of her professional dreams. On Friday, she will attempt to make 135 pounds for the fourth time in a grueling process that demands every ounce of her discipline and commitment.  
"I don't know if you can ever master cutting weight," Harrison said. "I don't know if that's ever a thing. But I do have a remarkable team behind me. This has been the 'least stressful' weight cut so far, but it is what it is."
Both Harrison and Nunes didn't have a bad word to say about each other for the vast majority of the fight's promotion, as both appear to have decided that any lingering negativity that may or may not have fueled Nunes' ATT exit some five years into their tenure as teammates isn't worth rehashing. Many of their former coaches and teammates, however, tell a different story. "We only sparred one time. It was before I had [officially] moved to American Top Team and I hadn't had a fight yet," Harrison said. "I had been training for a couple months, and I was trying out different gyms. My second day [at ATT] was sparring day with Amanda."So, what happened in the sparring match? "No, no, that's a faux pas," Harrison said. "We don't talk about what happened in sparring. But, I mean, clearly I had never fought before. It's not like I walked in there and absolutely thrashed her."
Harrison was often asked, even before her pro debut, by media members whether she would ever want to fight Nunes. Each and every time, Harrison said yes. "I think that was probably what rubbed Amanda the wrong way," Harrison said. "I wasn't bringing it up, but I would say, 'Of course I would want to fight her. She's the greatest of all time.' To me, that's a compliment. If [UFC bantamweight and teammate] Bea [Mesquita] does an interview and says she wants to fight me, I don't take that as a threat. I take that as a compliment. Of course, you should want to fight me."Harrison remains steadfast that she never looked at their training relationship as anything but a chance to make each other better. Still, the two eventually stopped working together once Harrison began establishing herself as a dominant pro fighter, and most still believe that Harrison's presence had a lot to do with Nunes' eventual decision to start her own gym.  
"You have to ask Amanda that. I'm not in her head," Harrison said. "We don't talk about it, and it's not like I'm texting her about it. I was very much a team player. I never felt threatened or that there was a scarcity of coaches. That's one of the reasons that I trained there, because of her. If you want to be the best, you have to train with the best. By the time I got to work with her, it was a great opportunity for me. I feel like we are both very respectful, and it never got nasty. "I have nothing bad to say about Amanda, but I'm just a loyal person. I started my career at ATT and I'm going to end my career at ATT. The same four guys are going to be in my corner on Saturday night, as they were on my first fight and I'm happy with that."At Thursday's final press conference, the mask of restraint previously worn by Harrison and Nunes finally came off as the two engaged in an extended argument about why their training relationship fell apart. Nunes accused Harrison of not being honest about wanting to fight her from the beginning and Harrison ended the public spat by declaring that their ATT coaches only separated them from training with one another because "they were trying to protect you from me." 
Quoting her longtime judo coach, Jimmy "Big Jim" Pedro Sr., Harrison believes Saturday's fight is a battle between a racehorse and a workhorse or, in fight terms, a classic matchup between a powerful striker and a grinding wrestler. "I think we are so different as fighters, even in our training method," Harrison said. "She is wicked talented, very gifted. She's a thoroughbred and I'm a workhorse. She has amazing knockouts and great highlights and I'm more of a gritty, grind-it-out type fighter. So, it's kind of a classic matchup in that sense but it ends with my hand raised."

title: Rory McIlroy leads DP World Tour Championship with eyes on Race to Dubai crown - CBS Sports
description: McIlroy is halfway to winning yet another season-long crown in Europe
body:
McIlroy is halfway to winning yet another season-long crown in Europe
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Nov 13, 2026
                            
                    at
    10:35 am ET
                        
                •
            
            3 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        No other name stands above Rory McIlroy's in either the season-long race or the DP World Tour Championship through two rounds of the European circuit's season finale. McIlroy's 36-hole total of 5 under par positions him atop the leaderboard alongside Englishman Tyrrell Hatton, which in turn gives McIlroy the projected lead in the Race to Dubai heading into the weekend at Jumeirah Golf Estates.McIlroy entered the week No. 2 in the Race to Dubai standings behind Eugenio Chacarra as he aims to capture his eighth season-long crown on the DP World Tour. As it stands, McIlroy is one behind Colin Montgomerie for the most all-time after claiming the title in each of the last four seasons.The world No. 2 got off to a beautiful start on Friday as he turned in 3 under and tacked on another birdie on the gettable par-4 10th. The Earth Course bit back, however, as McIlroy carded three bogeys on his back nine, including back-to-back squares on Nos. 16-17 and fell out of the lead momentarily.He would recover on the final hole, though, with a two-putt birdie to set up a date with Hatton in the final group in the third round.
"If anything, I started to get frustrated with the golf course," McIlroy said. "It just, you know, as it dries out, lies and fairways aren't very good, and greens start to get bumpy. And I started to get maybe a little bit frustrated with the course on the way in. But I think it's just the nature of it. It's a tough test. "I think, as well, I've been coming to this golf course for 17 years, and this is the toughest I think it's ever played. So in my mind it's sort of like, well, you should be going out and shooting 66 or 65, and the course just isn't set up that way this week. And you just have to show a little bit more patience out there."
McIlroy may have Hatton alongside him on Saturday, but he will be keeping one eye on the young Spaniard. Chacarra has experienced a volatile two days in Dubai, but he finished Friday on a high note as a birdie on the par-3 17th was followed by a chip-in birdie on the par-5 finisher.
The 26-year-old is only four strokes behind McIlroy at 1 under and in a tie for 11th place. Through two rounds, Chacarra has carded 10 birdies and nine bogeys and still has a very real chance to fend off McIlroy."It's just what it is. I knew it was going to happen," Chacarra said. "It's one of the favorite courses of Rory, and he's had so much success in here. He's obviously one of the best players in the world. So, we know it's going to be tough. "There's two rounds of golf; 36 holes is a lot. And, yeah, I like how I'm hitting it. There's been a lot of birdies in harder conditions. So, if I can clean up the card a little, I like my chance on the weekend."
Another name to keep an eye on as the proceedings continue is that of Jon Rahm. A winner last week in Abu Dhabi, Rahm has signed for back-to-back 71s and is in a tie for eighth place with two rounds to play. The two-time major champion is a three-time winner of this event, all of which featured a comeback of similar proportions at the halfway mark.Although Rahm did not play full-time on the DP World Tour this season, he still has a chance to take down the Race to Dubai thanks to his win at the Abu Dhabi Championship. "I'm making really good swings. I'm playing really good golf," Rahm said. "Yesterday … those swings weren't giving me the results I wanted off the tee. Today was more so the irons. I felt like I was making good swings. 
"A great example would be 17. Loads of wind in and off the left, and I hit a little fade that somehow the wind never moved. So one of those days that can happen. And days like today, swirls, etc., all we can do is keep putting good swings in. And I feel like I've done that and hit a lot of good putts. Hopefully I start hitting them a little closer on the weekend."

title: Grading every NFL team at the midway point: Chargers get an 'F,' three teams get solid 'A' grade - CBS Sports
description: Buffalo is among the highest-rated teams, while the Eagles sit at the opposite end as a big disappointment
body:
Buffalo is among the highest-rated teams, while the Eagles sit at the opposite end as a big disappointment

            10 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        We're just past the midway point of the NFL season, which means it's time to start thinking seriously about who has and has not met the expectations we set for them at the start of the year. Everyone came into the season with a different set of hopes, and everyone has had plenty of time to meet, exceed or fall short of them now that we have played nine weeks of football.For some teams, whether they have done what was expected of them is fairly obvious: The Chargers have not, for example. For other teams, it's not so obvious: The entire NFC South would fit that description. But what about the rest of the teams in the league? How have they performed, and how would we grade them relative to what was expected of them entering the season? 
That's why we're here. We're assigning letter grades to each team's performance through the midway point of the season. We broke down where each team stands, and why, below.TeamGradeComment
                            
    
                                                
                    
    C-Dallas came into this season with high hopes but has instead disappointed. The Cowboys' defense remains a disaster, and the offense hasn't lived up to expectations. They've also blown a couple of games with poor situational football awareness. The only thing saving them from a worse grade is that the rest of the NFC East is bad enough that they're in second place and potentially in position to make a run at the playoffs.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    ANotwithstanding their Thursday night loss to Washington, the Giants could hardly have hoped for the start of the John Harbaugh era to go any better results-wise. They're in first place in the division despite having lost their starting quarterback in the second game of the season. Rookie Arvell Reese looks like a total monster. They have mostly won close games, so they might not be as good as their record indicates, but that doesn't matter when it comes to how they've performed relative to expectations.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    DThe Eagles would have an F if not for Howie Roseman's smart pivot to selling off pieces at and around the trade deadline, which restocked the cupboard full of draft picks for the future. Philly is always smart about knowing when to pull the plug on a lost season, which is exactly what this year has been.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    CThe Commanders weren't necessarily expected to be all that competitive in the NFC East this year, but the degree to which they've fallen behind the Giants and Cowboys is disappointing. The game management issues under Dan Quinn have also persisted, which contributes to this grade.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    A-The Bears, like the rest of the NFC North, have to be happy with how their season has gone to date. The offense looks explosive, and the defense looks better after the addition of Jeffery Simmons. The only thing holding them back from getting a straight 'A' here is the surprising lack of run game efficiency, though Kyle Monangai's absence has contributed to that. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    A-The Lions have one of the most explosive offenses in the league, with Jahmyr Gibbs, Amon-Ra St. Brown, Jameson Williams and Sam LaPorta combining with Jared Goff to light up scoreboards. The defense has even been playing better lately, albeit in light matchups. There have been some issues here and there (like the loss to the Panthers), but overall, things have gone quite well relative to expectations.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    A-The Packers have to be thrilled with how their season has gone. Despite the absence of Micah Parsons, the defense has been excellent. Jordan Love is playing near an MVP level. Christian Watson and Matthew Golden look like superstars. The one thing holding them back from an 'A' is how they started the season, with a bad loss to Minnesota and the blowout against Atlanta. Otherwise, things have gone about as well as could be expected.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    A-The Vikings' defense gets an A+++++, but the offense has been bad enough to knock the team down nearly a full letter grade despite Minnesota's 6-2 record. Here's hoping that Kirk Cousins can at least prop things up a bit for the rest of the season.

    C+The Cardinals have actually been better than anybody expected. They have three wins, and they've played a couple of other close games mixed in there. They do have five double-digit losses, though, so it's hard to give them a grade in the 'B' range. Things will also likely get worse the rest of the way, given their injury issues. That said, getting a second-round pick back for Marvin Harrison Jr. looks like a good deal.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    C-The Super Team expectations were probably always a bit too high, but the Rams haven't come close for a variety of reasons. Whether it's injuries, Matthew Stafford's regression or even more injuries, you have to dock the Rams for not even being a surefire playoff team at the midpoint of the season. Being over .500 despite the injuries is mildly impressive, but not enough to give them a grade in the 'B' range.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    AThe 49ers are a team that has overcome nearly as many injuries as the Rams have faced. It seems like as long as they have Kyle Shanahan, Brock Purdy, Christian McCaffrey and George Kittle, they are just going to keep humming. And Raheem Morris has the defense playing well despite its own injury issues. They've been great on both sides of the ball.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    C+We initially had the Seahawks at a 'B-' grade, but then we remembered the odd loss to the Commanders in Week 3 and had to knock them down. Seattle has navigated some offseason losses (Klint Kubiak, Kenneth Walker III and more) and injury issues (the entire backfield), and three of its four losses came in one-score games, but we expected the Seahawks to be closer to the top of the division than they are right now.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    AThe Bills have overcome a questionable defense to emerge midway through the season with a 7-1 record. Josh Allen is firmly in the MVP mix once again. James Cook is averaging even more rushing yards per game than he did a year ago. The offense has kept humming despite DJ Moore missing time. The Joe Brady era is off to a very good start.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    CThe Dolphins have played right around expectations so far this year. They have smartly played at a snail's pace on offense to try and shorten games and stay competitive, which has resulted in them losing by less than expected in some contests, and they even beat the Jets. Still, it's hard to justify better than a 'C' grade when you're 1-7 at the halfway point.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    B-The Patriots' start to the season was terrible. They then got on a little bit of a run to bounce back, and it looked like they might recapture some of what they had last year. But they've lost two games against good teams over the last three weeks, and they got smacked by the Packers in the most recent one. The injury issues on offense matter, but sitting at 5-4 before their trip to Munich is a slight disappointment.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    C+The Jets look like they have a nice corps of young players on both offense and defense, but they're also 2-7. It's hard to find the appropriate grade for that type of team, especially when it's coming off its worst loss of the season, where it was totally non-competitive. It feels like a 'C+' is just right, relative to what we expected from them coming into this year.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    C+Considering they haven't had Lamar Jackson for much of the season (he basically played 3.5 games), it's at least somewhat impressive that the Ravens are still in the mix in the AFC at 4-5. But they've lost four games in a row and have looked inept offensively of late (albeit in brutal situations), and Jesse Minter's defense hasn't been able to make up for it. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    A-The Bengals' offense started the season somewhat slowly, as per usual, but has kicked into high gear of late, as per usual. Joe Burrow, Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins are basically unstoppable, and the defense is improved relative to recent years. There have been some ups and downs with that unit (27 points against the Bucs despite four turnovers, 30 against the Steelers, 24 against the Dolphins despite three turnovers, 36 against the Titans despite two turnovers), so that's keeping them from earning a straight 'A' here. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    B+The Browns are 5-4, which would make you think they should get an 'A' relative to expectations. But when you look at the context of those games, and the fact that they each required a game-winning drive in the final five minutes, you see that the record isn't as impressive as it looks on the surface. Still, the wins count, and five is probably more than many people expected them to get coming into the year.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    B+The inexcusable loss to the Browns back in Week 4 keeps the Steelers out of the 'A' range, which they might otherwise be in, given their offense and defense. The run game has been impressive, and the defense has maintained a high level of play. Coming out of their bye at 6-2 is an ideal midseason result.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    C-The Texans are 3-5, and two of their wins have come against the Titans and Chargers. Their defense has regressed year over year. That all overshadows the great season they're getting out of C.J. Stroud, who has been even better this year than he was during his spectacular rookie season. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    D-The Colts have been a disaster on both sides of the ball and had to enter fire-sale mode. This grade would be lower if not for the fact that they did get some assets for a few players who were obviously on their way out the door. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    A-The Jaguars are 6-2 with two one-score losses, and they look elite on both offense and defense. They might have an inside track on the No. 1 seed in the AFC, given their rest-of-season strength of schedule. We docked them to an 'A-' thanks only to the frankly bonkers price they paid in the Jordan Davis trade, even if he is going to help their defense the rest of the way.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    C-The Titans looked more competent in their final three games going into their Week 9 bye, even if they did lose two of them. The offense looked so bad early in the year, though, that we can't even justify giving them a straight 'C' here. We're grading the entire season to date, not just what's happened most recently. Getting a second-round pick and more for Amani Hooker was nice, though.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    A-I don't know how the Broncos keep getting away with it in one-score games (6-0 this season), but they do. They're probably not as good as their 6-2 record suggests, and they got embarrassed in the season opener against Kansas City, but there's no denying their track record of winning in clutch situations at this point. So, we're giving them a bit of credit for it here. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    B+The Chiefs have taken care of business for the most part this season, losing only to the Seahawks and Broncos on the road in back-to-back weeks. They have otherwise been able to run the ball at will on everyone, and their defense has been excellent. The blip in Weeks 7 and 8 counts, though, and it revealed an inability to find a way to win if Kenneth Walker doesn't go off. That matters.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    BThings worked out quite nicely for the Raiders. They started out 3-0, Kirk Cousins played well enough to give Fernando Mendoza time to sit and learn for half a season, and then they got a third-round pick for Cousins at the deadline. If they hadn't lost five of their last six games, this grade would be even higher.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    FNo need to elaborate on this one.

title: One fatal flaw of every Super Bowl contender from 49ers depth to Packers run game - CBS Sports
description: Normally, when I write, I deal in optimism. Giving fans a reason for hope, something to look forward to when their favorite team takes t
body:
Normally, when I write, I deal in optimism. Giving fans a reason for hope, something to look forward to when their favorite team takes the field.Today is not one of those days.The NFL trade deadline has come and gone, and while most teams have improved their chances at winning a Super Bowl, I'm here to pour a little bit of cold water on the excitement. No team is perfect, especially this year, when it feels like there's much more parity across the board. While there are obvious Super Bowl contenders, even those teams have flaws that could stop them from hoisting the Lombardi Trophy come February. Let's break down the fatal flaw of every contender at midseason, and if it comes true, then you can blame me.*Contenders chosen using DraftKings Sportsbook midseason Super Bowl odds
                            
    
                                                
                    
    San Francisco 49ers: DepthI'm convinced the 49ers are living their own separate version of the movie "Groundhog Day." Every year they come in as legitimate contenders, then it all unravels because of injury. Well, this year is no different, with their depth already being tested.On the defensive side of the ball, standout rookie DT Gracen Halton is going to miss the rest of the season with a broken ankle, and CBs Deommodore Lenoir and Renardo Green are both nursing foot injuries (but those are more day-to-day, according to Kyle Shanahan). Offensively, WR Mike Evans hasn't played since week 6, and WR Deebo Samuel hasn't played since week 5. They've gotten by with playing WRs Jordan Watkins, Brandin Cooks and Demarcus Robinson , but that's not a Super Bowl-winning trio. However, they did recently trade for Keenan Allen.
The spin zone here is that the cavalry is coming for reinforcements. Adding DT DeForest Buckner before the trade deadline was a huge move for the defensive line, helping them get more pressure without blitzing (the 49ers are 30th in the NFL in blitz rate and 20th in sack rate without blitzing). I've been a fan of what DC Raheem Morris has been able to get out of this defense, playing to the speed at the second and third level, and adding Buckner to that group should let the secondary play even faster (losing Halton sucks, though). The more worrisome part is Evans, who is still more than likely not going to play against Dallas next week. Achilles tendinitis is scary, especially at Evans' age. He was such a critical part of why the Niners offense was back to the face-melting unit they've been in previous years, and if he can't go for the long haul, I worry about how this team can win the Super Bowl.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Buffalo Bills: Preventing explosive playsDespite adding safety Amani Hooker at the trade deadline, I still think the Bills' pass defense overall is the weakest part of the unit. As long as they don't get to play Carson Wentz every week, the Bills' pass defense is going to be what holds them back. 
The Bills' defensive line has been a revelation this season; with the growth of EDGE Greg Rousseau and DT Deone Walker, the Bills are eighth in the NFL in pressure rate. However, their splits when they're under pressure versus when they're not are staggering. According to TruMedia, when they get pressure, they have a 69.5% defensive success rate and 0.15 defensive EPA/dropback. Combine all plays where they force a PBU, INT, TFL and sack together when they get pressure, and you get a 21.9% havoc rate when recording a pressure. When they don't get pressure, their defensive success rate drops to 45.5% (only above the Raiders), -0.31 defensive EPA per dropback, and that havoc rate? Yeah, it drops to 11.4%. Not a great look for their coverage unit.The biggest problem is that they give up explosive plays, and while some of that should be ironed out by adding Hooker, I worry that DC Jim Leonhard just doesn't have the guys to prevent explosive plays in the middle of the field. If you just whittle it down to passing attempts between the hashmarks in the middle of the field, they've given up the second most completions of 20 or more yards in that area in the NFL. If they can't limit big plays, I worry about how much will be on the offense to keep cleaning up the defense's mistakes.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Jacksonville Jaguars: Offensive lineThe Jacksonville Jaguars have arrived. After starting the season 6-2, the Jaguars made a massive splash at the trade deadline, acquiring S Jessie Bates and DT Jordan Davis to shore up two of their bigger issues on the defensive line. However, if this team falls before winning a Super Bowl, it'll be because of their pass protection. 
On the surface, the Jaguars' offensive line looks good. They're tied for the fifth-lowest sacks allowed this season and eighth-lowest pressure rate allowed. On top of that, the Jaguars' ability to grind games down by running the football has been evident this season. However, digging into those numbers and watching the Jaguars play tells a different story. In the passing game, Trevor Lawrence has been incredible this season at mitigating pressure and getting the ball out (a major part of his MVP case). Then, in the run game, the Jaguars are only above the Raiders in average yards before contact per carry, at 0.68 (their yards after contact per carry are 3.40, 6th in the NFL). The offensive line has been overwhelmed by interior pressure, with rookie LG Emmanuel Pregnon and RG Ezra Cleveland up and down in pass protection. Starting LT Anton Harrison has been lost for the season, and while Walker Little has performed admirably in his absence, it'll always be a worry for the Jaguars.Lawrence has, like I said, been amazing at mitigating pressure and making plays around it. But in order to get out of the AFC, they'll have to face guys like Zach Allen, Dexter Lawrence, Cameron Heyward and more. If this team doesn't get to the Super Bowl, it'll be because the offensive line fell apart.

                            
    
                                                
                    
    Chicago Bears: SecondaryThe Bears and the Jaguars back-to-back in Super Bowl contender stories — what a beautiful world we live in. The Bears look like one of the most complete teams in the NFL, with an offense that can score at will or grind teams into dust. To complement that offense, the Bears added a nitro boost to the defense by trading for DT Jeffrey Simmons, and that trade already looks like it paid off. However, if this team doesn't win the whole thing this year, it'll be because of a secondary that has been…volatile to say the least.This isn't to say the Bears' secondary isn't talented. Kyler Gordon is an awesome nickel, and I've been impressed with the play of rookie Malik Muhammad on the outside. However, Muhammad has missed the last two games with a toe injury, leaving the Bears thin in the secondary. The mainstay of the group, CB Jaylon Johnson, has been inconsistent this season as well. I was of the belief that the Bears should've added another corner at the deadline to just give them some more insurance, but by not adding anyone, it shows a lot of belief in that group. I wouldn't believe in that group as much, and if they don't win it all, it'll be because the secondary fell apart.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Kansas City Chiefs: Creating explosive passesI never thought I'd say this about a Patrick Mahomes-led unit, but the Chiefs' passing game isn't very explosive. Kansas City is only 21st in the NFL in completions of 20 or more yards this season, despite having a high rate of explosive passes. That is probably because only 14.4% of Patrick Mahomes' passing attempts this season are between 11 and 20 air yards, and only 8.4% are over 20 air yards, both near the bottom of the NFL. 
Without WR Tyquan Thornton on the field, there's nobody who can win on passes downfield. Among all the Chiefs receivers this season, Thornton still leads the team in receptions of at least 16 or more air yards, despite going down in Week 4. Xavier Worthy leads the team in targets in that metric, but he only has two catches at that range. Not being able to hit any explosives makes the offense so much more congested, leaving the run game too little space to breathe and allowing opposing defenses to squat on all the crossing routes Kansas City likes to run.The Chiefs did add a receiver at the deadline, trading for Indy's Josh Downs. Where Downs will help is in creating separation against man coverage and loosening up the offense in the intermediate game so Rice can be the over-the-top and YAC guy. But this team is still missing that third gear downfield. Worthy hasn't been consistent and is now out with a hamstring injury, so adding someone with size and speed in free agency could be key (Darius Slayton could be fun). Maybe the hope is that the run game provides the explosives, which is definitely possible. But if the Chiefs fail to win the Super Bowl for the third straight year, it'll be because they can't create any explosive passes.

                            
    
                                                
                    
    Cincinnati Bengals: Shaky linebacker playThis Bengals team feels like a warm hug, a truly vintage Burrow-era Bengals unit. One of the most face-melting offenses the NFL has seen (doing it without even wanting to run the ball or getting under center), and a field-tilting defensive lineman who can absolutely take over. However, if this team isn't raising the Lombardi at the end of the season, it'll be because of some real shoddy linebacker play. The trio of Barrett Carter, Demetrius Knight Jr and Oren Burks doesn't exactly inspire confidence, especially when it comes to pass coverage. All three guys are better at flowing fast downhill and creating negative plays in the run game, but their eyes can be manipulated in coverage. The Bengals are tied for the fifth-most plays of over 20 yards allowed on play action in the NFL this season, and in both of their losses, the Bengals linebackers have been poor in coverage. Because they are fitting the run so aggressively, they leave themselves susceptible to explosives in the middle of the field off play action, which is where every team is trying to hunt in the NFL.If you look at all the teams in the AFC, they're all incredible at manipulating linebackers via play action and getting wires crossed. For the Bengals to beat teams like Buffalo, Jacksonville, Kansas City and Pittsburgh, their linebacker play needs to improve in pass coverage. I'm a little surprised they didn't try to add to the linebacker room at the trade deadline, but given how their first trade went down, it makes sense they bowed out after that. Either way, their linebacker play hasn't been up to par this season, and it could be their downfall.

                            
    
                                                
                    
    Los Angeles Rams: Inefficient downfield passingIf I had a nickel for every time an NFL "Superteam" was unraveled by injury and poor play, I'd have two nickels. That's not a lot, but the fact that it happened twice is relevant. The Rams have gone from being everyone's Super Bowl favorite to being on the brink of missing the playoffs entirely, a cataclysmic drop that will have many people asking what happened. Aside from the obvious caveat that everyone important on the team has been hurt at some point this season, I think the biggest reason this team hasn't been the same unit is that they can't hit explosive passes. Take this as a comparison: According to TruMedia, the Rams had a 15.9% explosive pass rate last season, good for sixth in the NFL. In 2026, that number has dropped to 10.8%, below teams like the Miami Dolphins and Pittsburgh Steelers. Now, part of that has legitimately been due to injuries to players like WR Davante Adams, TE Terrance Ferguson and now WR Puka Nacua, but Matthew Stafford just hasn't been accurate outside the numbers this season. A large part of their explosive offense last year was Stafford catching fire on those passes, drilling corners and out routes to stop defenses from congesting the middle of the field. 
Overall, TruMedia has Stafford's off-target rate jumping up three percentage points this season, but when you specify passes on the sideline or outside the numbers, his off-target rate has jumped from 15% in 2025 to 28.6% this season. That's an alarming uptick in inaccuracy, one that is telling for an older QB like Stafford. If he can't drill those passes, the offense becomes much more difficult. If the Rams want to make the playoffs, they need to get healthy. If they want to win a Super Bowl, Stafford has to hit those passes more often.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Denver Broncos: Inconsistent Passing GameAs it currently stands, the Broncos have a 37.1% passing success rate, 28th in the NFL. Since 2010, the worst passing offense to win a Super Bowl by that metric is the 2015 Denver Broncos…who were at 42.2%. It would be historically unprecedented for a team with as bad a passing offense as the Broncos to win the Super Bowl, and it's by far the Broncos' biggest flaw. Now, I will add that every year the Broncos' passing game starts off slow and then picks up by the time the playoffs roll around, and so far this season that's proven to be the case. However, I still think the passing offense is far too inconsistent for me to trust them in close game scenarios.
For the Broncos to win the Super Bowl, Nix has to consistently hit the designed passes in the middle of the field. He's done a better job of that recently than in previous weeks, but against healthy secondaries I worry that the offense will turtle back on itself and not allow Sean Payton's well-designed offense to click. Everything is in position for this offense to once again hit their late-season surge, but if they want to win a Super Bowl, the passing game needs to start clicking.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Seattle Seahawks: Lack of explosive runsEveryone is wondering what's wrong with the Seahawks' offense this season. Is it a decline from QB Sam Darnold? OC Brian Fleury doesn't pull the same levers as Klint Kubiak did? Is it just general regression? In a way, all of these are correct, but the root of the problem is that they aren't an explosive running team this season. Last year, while the Seahawks' run game wasn't "great" (-0.04 EPA per carry, 39.5% rushing success rate on all designed runs), they had a 7.3% explosive rushing rate. This season, the Seahawks' run game has fallen off a cliff, putting up a putrid -0.20 EPA per carry, 33.5% rushing success rate and a 6.2% explosive rushing rate. Even last season when the Seahawks' run game wasn't exactly the most efficient, you could count on at least a few explosive runs from their offense to keep the thought in defenses' heads and make the game easier on Darnold. Without any explosive runs AND being inefficient, the Seahawks consistently put themselves behind the sticks and in obvious passing situations, where Darnold doesn't thrive.There is a solution to this problem: Quenton Nelson. The Seahawks traded for the LG before the deadline, and he looked as advertised before going down with an injury. Once he and LT Charles Cross get back, the run game could improve. But if the Seahawks fail to repeat, you can blame the lack of explosive runs.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Detroit Lions: Secondary playRemember earlier when I said the Bills have a problem preventing explosive plays? Ditto for the Lions, who have been hit by the injury bug once again. Despite getting S Brian Branch back, the secondary still has issues with defending the pass. Per Sumer Sports, the Lions are 22nd in the NFL in passing success rate allowed and 28th in EPA/pass allowed. The biggest issue has come when they play man coverage, leaving their cornerbacks on islands. CB DJ Reed has made the occasional big play, but CB Rock Ya-Sin has been targeted often, as has Roger McCreary. The back-end coverage play has undone what has been a very good season for their defensive front, preventing them from getting home and making plays.The Lions' offense is Super Bowl caliber, and I think their defensive line can play up to that level as well. But the depth on this team continues to be tested, and now without LB Jack Campbell and S Kerby Joseph, getting by in the secondary will just have to do.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Green Bay Packers: The worst rushing offense in footballI'm not joking when I say the Packers' rushing offense is one of the worst units in football this year. Through nine games, the only three teams worse than Green Bay on the ground based on rushing success rate are the Miami Dolphins, Las Vegas Raiders and Cleveland Browns (per TruMedia). If we use EPA per rush, the Packers are dead last. Now there are multiple symptoms for this, and they're all bad. The offensive line can't get enough push to run the gap scheme runs the Packers want to get into (29th in yards before contact per carry), and the Packers' RBs have also given the team next to nothing when it comes to making people miss. As a team, the Packers are 30th in yards after contact per carry and 27th in percentage of tackles avoided. The offensive line has been unsettled since losing RT Zach Bako-Bewele to injury, and because they haven't had a chance to find their best five, the run game has been awful. Combine that with the running back room not having any form of juice, and you get needing WR Savion Williams to be your best threat running the football.With QB Jordan Love and the defense playing as well as they are right now, it should be easy to call the Packers a Super Bowl team. But if they don't make it there, it'll be because they can't run the football and make it easier on themselves.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Minnesota Vikings: Everything about the offenseSince 2000, there have been 379 teams with winning records through nine games. The 2026 Minnesota Vikings rank 379th in offensive success rate.We could end this right there, but let's dig into why every time the Vikings offense takes the field, it feels like a win for the other team. First of all, the accuracy of any QB under center has been erratic. This season, among QBs with at least 50 dropbacks, both Kyler Murray and Carson Wentz are in the top 10 in off-target rate per TruMedia. The Minnesota offense doesn't have a lot of built-in easy buttons for throwing the football; much of it is about attacking vertically and pushing the ball to hunt explosives. So when these plays are missing, you dig yourself into a lot of second/third and longs. You can offset this by using your run game, always staying ahead of the sticks and freeing your QB to take downfield shots because you know you can get 4-5 yards on the ground. Well, the Vikings sit at 29th in rushing success rate and average the second-lowest yards after contact per carry in the NFL. So if you're not accurate and you can't run the ball either, you get an easy recipe for one of the worst offenses the NFL has ever seen (no exaggeration!)
The Vikings traded for QB Kirk Cousins on Tuesday, and while I think he'll definitely help by throwing fewer inaccurate passes, I do wonder if he is enough to get this team over the hump. Cousins isn't a spring chicken and has already thrown a lot of passes this season, so his arm might just be shot at this point. If the Vikings can't get a run game going, Cousins might not matter at all.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    New England Patriots: Lack of depth at receiverIt's unfortunate that WRs AJ Brown and Romeo Doubs went down with multiple injuries this season, because if any team has needed both of them, it's the New England Patriots. After seemingly finding their groove, the music fell to a screeching halt against Green Bay. Drake Maye had another game of multiple interceptions, and the Patriots lost by 30 points. Their receiver group has been subpar to this point in the season, leaning on Mack Hollins and Pop Douglas once again. Because there are no easy buttons in this offense, it's all on Maye to keep the offense afloat, and that hasn't gone well this season. They were never going to be in the receiver market this trade deadline, but I wouldn't be surprised if they made a move in free agency, just to give Maye some more help.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Pittsburgh Steelers: Lack of separation in the offenseI'm sometimes confused by the Steelers' offense. They're at their best when they play through the offensive line, RBs Jaylen Warren and Rico Dowdle, and the mammoths they have at tight end. But then they try to spread teams out and shred them that way. This doesn't work because the Steelers lack separation on offense, especially at receiver. WR DK Metcalf has been wildly inconsistent this season, mixing in explosive receptions and great blocking with the most baffling drops you've ever seen. WR Michael Pittman Jr. has been on IR since October, and even when he comes back, you don't expect him to be a separator in the offense. Nobody in the Steelers' receiving room is a big enough threat against man coverage to be a problem, and it shrinks the Rolodex of options the offense can get to in third down or obvious passing situations. Swinging and missing on a receiver at the deadline is brutal, and if they don't win a Super Bowl this year, the skill position group will be why.

title: Fantasy Baseball 2027: Grant Taylor leads bullpen-to-rotation candidates - CBS Sports

body:
Not everyone can be a starting pitcher. It's an oversimplification to say every reliever is just a failed starter, but it's only a mild oversimplification. Starters are asked to shoulder a much heavier burden than relievers, even now, and being able to both physically hold up to a starter's workload and get through a lineup multiple times while remaining effective is a combination few pitchers can routinely manage. Because of this, no team in baseball ever has enough starting pitching. Nope, that team you're thinking of? They don't have enough starting pitching, even if it looks like they do right now. They don't. Or, at least, they won't. MLB teams can't develop them fast enough in the minors to replace the ones who are getting hurt and falling apart in the majors, in large part because the guys in the minors are also getting hurt and falling apart. This inevitably leads them back to the relief pitcher class. Teams have grown more aggressive about moving pitchers from the bullpen back to the rotation in recent years, and we've seen some very high-profile success stories in that regard. Garrett Crochet is probably the most notable, but we saw success stories in the form of Reid Detmers, Griffin Jax, and Justin Wrobleski in 2026, and names like Michael King, Nick Pivetta, Clay Holmes, Nick Martinez, and Seth Lugo over the past half-decade or so, too. In part, that's because expectations for starters keep getting lowered – nobody is throwing 110 pitches every time out these days, and few starters are even asked to throw 180 innings in a season now. 
But, given the proliferation of mountains of data about pitching in the past decade or so, we also just have a better understanding of which pitchers have the stuff to move back to the rotation. Add in the growth of pitch design labs around baseball, and teams are much more able to be aggressive about taking shots with pitchers who move from the bullpen to the rotation.What does that look like? And who might get the call for 2027? We'll try to answer both questions today, first by looking back at what has happened with reliever-to-starter conversions, and then by projecting who might be able to make it work in the future. To start with, let's look at 25 pitchers between 2021 and 2026 who threw at least 50 innings as a reliever in one season and then followed that up with at least 50 innings as a starter in the following season, focusing on what those pitchers' velocities looked like in each role, and what the quality of their arsenals looked like, based on the Stuff+ metric on FanGraphs.com (which takes into account the physical characteristics of each pitch in a pitcher's arsenal to try to quantify, well, the quality of their stuff, where 100 is average):
The key takeaways here are mostly what you'd expect: Pitchers lose something moving from the bullpen to the rotation. On average, a pitcher's Stuff+ drops about eight points, from an above-average mark to a slightly below-average one. That comes along with an average drop of about 1.4 mph of fastball velocity, though neither is the same for every player. For example, Clay Holmes' Stuff+ dropped from 126 to 100 when he made the leap, while Cristian Javier actually went from roughly average to elite stuff in his full season as a starter. Every situation is different, and the results aren't always what you'd expect, either – Nick Martinez has seen his stuff collapse from 2023 to 2024, only to more or less hold steady from 2024 to 2025.But the general direction is clear, and there is usually some kind of penalty. Pitchers can make up for it with a widened arsenal or improved command, but as a general rule, you should expect a pitcher to be less effective in a starting role than as a reliever. Obviously. 
With this in mind, let's take a look at eight candidates to make the move from the bullpen to the rotation, and what we might expect from them for Fantasy in 2027. Reliever conversion candidatesGrant Taylor, White Sox2026 Stuff+ rating: 104; Translated Stuff+ as SP: 98Taylor is the one we know for sure will be making the transition, and with that in mind … this is kind of underwhelming? But it might be underselling him. He averaged 98 mph with his four-seamer, but he did that while recording more than three outs in 31 of his 60 appearances. He made a postseason appearance in which he tossed 54 pitches over 2.1 innings with five strikeouts, averaging 97.5 mph on the four-seamer; he followed that up with six strikeouts over four innings, averaging 98.1 mph in his very next outing. His four-seamer was his primary strikeout weapon, though, so any diminishment of velocity or shape could affect him more than most pitchers. Taylor has a four-pitch arsenal, but he doesn't necessarily have a go-to weapon against left-handed hitters. That wasn't much of an issue in 2026 (he actually had a higher strikeout rate against lefties than righties), but it's one thing to watch for as he makes the transition. I would guess we'll hear reports this offseason about him working on a changeup, a cutter or both. 
Taylor's translated Stuff+ is still right around average, but honestly, that doesn't necessarily pass the sniff test for me. I don't think he's likely to be an ace, but the upside is there. His early ADP is right around 100 overall, which made sense when you could project him as a closer, but is way too rich with the question marks as a starter. Keep in mind, the 84 innings he threw in 2026 (92.2 including the playoffs) are by far a career high; he had never even hit 70 innings at any level prior. I think I'd be willing to make the bet on Taylor as a top-60 starting pitcher, probably closer to 150 in drafts. If he remains around 100th overall, it'll be pretty easy to pass on him, personally, with these question marks and a likely innings limit around 140 or 150. Didier Fuentes, Braves2026 Stuff+ rating: 116; Translated Stuff+ as SP: 108It is a bit surprising that Fuentes rates out better than Taylor by this measure, I'll admit. Both basically feature a three-pitch mix – Taylor has two fastballs, which he throws a combined 56% of the time, along with a slider and a curveball. At the same time, Fuentes leans on his four-seamer 69% of the time, with sliders around a quarter of the time and the occasional splitter. Neither necessarily has a fully well-rounded arsenal, but Fuentes' combo of a breaking ball plus an off-speed pitch might beat out Taylor's dual-breaking-ball combo. 
But it's also at least a little bit because Fuentes' slider is just a devastatingly effective pitch, holding opposing hitters to a .175 expected wOBA in 2026 while generating whiffs 38% of the time, both better than either of Taylor's breakers. Fuentes kind of has the Spencer Strider starter kit here; his fastball doesn't have quite as much ride as Strider's did at its best, but he makes up for that with more horizontal run. That two-plane movement may not hold up quite as well as a bat-misser, but he missed plenty of bats while limiting damage on contact with it in his relief role, and the breaker looks like a potential wipeout pitch.Fuentes also does have a longer track record as a starter in the minors. He hasn't racked up a ton of innings as of his age-21 season, but he did get up to 75.2 innings in 2024, 70 in 2025, and 97 in 2026; Taylor's 92.2 innings in 2026 are the only time he has ever reached even 70. There will still be workload concerns for Fuentes, and his role is less certain than Taylor's at this point. Still, I have a little more faith in his ability to work effectively as a starter than Taylor, especially if the splitter continues to develop. It doesn't hurt that he also has a curveball he rarely used in 2026 but which rated out well when he threw it in his brief 2025 run. Adrian Morejon, Free Agent2026 Stuff+ rating: 129; Translated Stuff+ as SP: 121For some context, a 121 Stuff+ would have been second only to Jacob Misiorowski among starters, and his closest comp among lefties would probably be Chris Sale. Morejon could lose three ticks off his fastball and still have elite velocity for a left-handed starter. He has a devastating arsenal, complete with a slider that rates out as a plus pitch and a changeup that simply looked like one of the best pitches in the league in 2026; among all pitches thrown at least 300 times last season, only Mason Miller's slider had a higher whiff rate than Morejon's 56% rate with his changeup. The .127 expected wOBA allowed was the best of any pitch. 
And teams are reportedly interested in Morejon as a starter. The only catch? Morejon apparently prefers to remain a reliever. The soon-to-be 28-year-old came up as a starter as a prospect, but never made more than 16 starts in a season as he struggled to stay healthy before moving to the bullpen full time in 2023. If that report is true, you have to admire the rare level of self-awareness Morejon is showing here, but it would be a bummer not to get to see him at least try to be a starter because he might have true ace potential in that role.Instead, he seems likely to sign somewhere as a closer, and he should be one of the absolute best in baseball in that role coming off a 107-strikeout season with a 2.83 ERA and 1.08 WHIP. Aaron Ashby, Brewers2026 Stuff+ rating: 118; Translated Stuff+ as SP: 110Ashby has emerged over the past few seasons as one of the best left-handed pitchers in baseball, and he just threw 107.1 phenomenal innings in 2026, including one of the most dominant postseason runs we've ever seen from a reliever. He has a legitimate four-pitch mix, including weapons for batters of both handedness, and he was starting as recently as 2024. Moving him to the rotation feels like a slam dunk, no? 
But, as Jarrett Seidler noted in his excellent breakdown of Ashby over at BaseballProspectus.com a few weeks ago, the case isn't quite as obvious as it seems. Ashby struggled with severe command issues during his times as a starter and always pitched better in relief than in the rotation. And, for as much as the Brewers leaned on him in 2026, he hasn't really been used in a high-volume role in a while, with Seidler noting Ashby has faced more than 12 batters once since 2024. Ashby told manager Pat Murphy as recently as Game 1 of the World Series, "I still want to be a starter," per The Athletic. On another team, Ashby might be a lock to at least get a look early on as a starter. But the Brewers churn out serviceable pitching like few teams in baseball, and Ashby's flexibility out of the bullpen might be more valuable to them than an extra 50-60 or so less effective innings as a starter might be, especially with Trevor Megill looking like a pretty obvious trade candidate for an always cost-conscious franchise. If we get a sense Ashby will be moving to the rotation, he might be the most interesting option among these names. But I'm not counting on it at this point. Louis Varland, Blue Jays2026 Stuff+ rating: 115; Translated Stuff+ as SP: 107Cards on the table: I think there's basically zero chance the Blue Jays actually make this move. Varland put up a 4.06 ERA in Triple-A as a starter and flopped badly in the majors before he was moved to the bullpen, and he has been so effective in that role that he was one of the key pieces in the team's World Series run in 2025 and then won the AL Reliever of the Year award for 2026. 
But they would be doing themselves a disservice if they didn't at least consider it with Varland. He's throwing 3-5 mph harder than he did as a starter, and that mostly held even when he was used a whopping 18 times in the 2025 playoffs. With four pitches he throws at least 8% of the time (plus a sinker he could surely lean on more if needed), it's definitely a starter's arsenal, especially with a clearly putaway pitch against hitters of both handedness in his knuckle curve and changeup. He has held his elite velocity despite bigger workloads than most relievers, including 16 appearances in 2026 with at least four outs recorded. Varland might be too valuable to the Blue Jays' bullpen to justify the experiment. But it might be worth chasing, given the question marks in their rotation. Spencer Miles, Blue Jays2026 Stuff+ rating: 101; Translated Stuff+ as SP: 93Fair warning: The names get a lot less interesting from here on out. Miles is the most interesting of the remaining ones, but I'll admit this one is more about the eye test than anything. Miles wasn't used as a traditional reliever in 2026, anyway, starting eight games and averaging nearly two innings per appearance, so the translated Stuff+ there may carry a lower penalty for him than for some others. He showed off a solid combination of above-average strikeout skills and good control as a rookie, though when you dive into his arsenal, he's missing a true standout putaway pitch; his best whiff rate came on his four-seamer, at a good, but not elite 27%. He limited hard contact well, but that skill doesn't necessarily carry over from one season to the next the way something like strikeout rate does. 
There is one extenuating circumstance worth keeping in mind with Miles, however: 2026 was basically his first time pitching as a professional. Because of back surgery and then Tommy John, he has thrown just 23.1 innings since he was drafted in 2022, and he only made it onto a major-league roster because he was a Rule 5 pick. In that context, the fact that Miles more than held his own as a rookie looks a lot more impressive, doesn't it? Betting on Miles is a long shot, for sure. The track record here is largely nonexistent. But he also feels like a candidate for an unconventional career arc, so I'll definitely be keeping him in mind as a late-round sleeper if it looks like the Blue Jays are going to give him a real chance. Antonio Senzatela, Free Agent2026 Stuff+ rating: 104; Translated Stuff+ as SP: 96Believe it or not, Senzatela has actually somehow been worse away from Coors Field than he was there – 4.93 career ERA in Coors, compared to a 5.26 mark elsewhere. That might be enough to write this one off entirely, especially after he struggled so much following a trade to the Brewers in the second half of 2026. There is still some swing-and-miss upside with his four-seamer, cutter, and curveball combo, and I imagine some team will take a flier on him this offseason, but the track record doesn't provide much reason for optimism. If Senzatela is in someone's rotation next spring and his fastball is sitting around 97 mph again, I'll check back in. For now, I don't see much reason to be optimistic. Paul Blackburn, Free Agent 2026 Stuff+ rating: 100; Translated Stuff+ as SP: 92I'm only including Blackburn here because he's coming off a 1.59 ERA while pitching out of the Yankees' bullpen in 2026. He did that while striking out just 20.5% of opposing hitters with a walk rate near 10%, leading to a 3.68 xERA that shows how far over his head he was. I wouldn't be shocked if some team decides to give Blackburn a call as rotation depth, but I would be shocked if he mattered much for Fantasy in 2027.
